To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) managers in the manufacturing sector are more likely to hold the government responsible than those in the service sector; (2) the central government is held more responsible than the local government; (3) managers in the south are more likely to blame the central government, whereas managers in the north are more likely to assign blame to the local government; and (4) managers in the north blame the central government less for not passing stricter regulations than do managers in the south.

Chinese managers hold the central and local governments primarily responsible for not having passed and for not having effectively enforced environmental regulations and that economic organizations are held secondly responsible.

1) managers in all sectors hold the central and local governments primarily responsible for not having passed stronger environmental regulations and for not enforcing the regulations that have been passed, 2) managers in all three cities hold economic organizations primarily responsible for not complying with environmental regulations, and 3) managers in all regions and sectors hold the central government primarily responsible for not enforcing the environmental regulations that have been issued.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the allocation of responsibility among various actors in the environmental policy process and the implications of these allocations for the effectiveness of policy implementation.
the allocation of responsibility among institutions in China.
